“There is scarcely any desire to revive such a memory,” said Mr. Knightley, feelingly; and for a moment or two he seemed to have done so. “But I,” he added promptly, “who have not been enchanted in that way, must still see, hear, and remember. Emma is spoiled by being the cleverest of her family. At ten she had the misfortune of being able to answer questions that baffled her sister at seventeen. She was always quick and confident; Isabella was slow and shy. And ever since she was twelve, Emma has been mistress of the house and of you all. In her mother she lost the only person capable of coping with her. She inherits her mother’s talents, and must have been under her influence.”

“I should have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, to rely on your recommendation, had I left Mr. Woodhouse’s family and sought another situation; I do not think you would have spoken a kind word for me to anyone. I am sure you always regarded me as unsuitable for the position I held.”

“Yes,” he said, smiling. “You are better placed here; very fit for a wife, but not at all for a governess. Yet you have been preparing yourself to be an excellent wife all the time you were at Hartfield. You might not give Emma such a complete education as your abilities would seem to promise; but you were receiving a very good education from her, especially on the matrimonial point of submitting your own will and doing as you were bid; and if Weston had asked me to recommend a wife for him, I should certainly have named Miss Taylor.”

“Thank you. There will be little merit in making a good wife for a man like Mr. Weston.”

“Honestly, I fear you are rather wasted, and that with every disposition to bear, there will be nothing to bear. We shall not despair, however. Weston may become irritable from indulgent comfort, or his son may trouble him.”

“I hope not that. It is unlikely. No, Mr. Knightley, do not predict vexation from that quarter.”

“Not I, indeed. I only mention possibilities. I do not claim Emma’s genius for foretelling and guessing. I hope, with all my heart, that the young man may be a Weston in merit and a Churchill in fortune. —But Harriet Smith—I have not half done about Harriet Smith. I think her the very worst sort of companion that Emma could possibly have."
}
